vo: If you have sciatica, don’t buy your next pair of shoes just because someone says they’re the best for back pain.
picture: Medium side view: woman around 60–70 pauses while getting ready beside a chair, hand briefly resting on her lower back. Cut to the clinic presenter addressing camera at 'don’t buy'. No branded shoes in the discomfort shot.
notes: Cold open on movement, not a logo. Two shots. Keep discomfort restrained; do not depict a shoe causing nerve compression.

vo: Hokas. New Balance. Brooks.
picture: Three actual shoe packshots, one per spoken name. Identical neutral background, scale and lighting. Use the specific models that will appear later.
notes: Three hard cuts synchronized to the brand names. No red X or 'unsafe' labels.

vo: Before you spend money on another pair, there are three things you need to look at.
picture: Presenter raises three fingers; cut to overhead lineup of the shoes on a table.
notes: Brief punch-in on 'three'. The three criteria later are feel in motion, fit, and comfort across daily activities.

vo: Especially if you’re over sixty and already planning your day around how long you can stay on your feet.
picture: Woman looks at a handwritten errands list, then sits to put shoes on. Show list items such as groceries and lunch; avoid medical records.
notes: Use adult lifestyle casting consistent throughout. No walker is needed; the reference uses one, but this line does not require it.

vo: Number one, Hokas.
picture: Full-frame number card with a real Hoka shoe isolated in profile.
notes: 0.6–1.0 second card; continue into product close-up if voiceover lasts longer. This adapts the reference’s third shoe to first position.

vo: You see the cushioning, and you think: that has to feel better.
picture: Macro side view of the actual Hoka midsole. Hand presses normally on the shoe, followed by a seated try-on.
notes: Keep proportions accurate. No altered heel height, compression simulation, or exaggerated sinking.

vo: When you’re dealing with shooting pain down your leg, it’s understandable to want something soft underneath you.
picture: Return to presenter for empathy. Optional cutaway: neutral seated woman gently resting her hand on thigh. If anatomy is used, show an independently clinician-reviewed nerve-route illustration labeled 'Illustration', separate from any shoe.
notes: Use the symptom as audience context. Do not connect a competitor shoe to a glowing or damaged nerve.

vo: But softness is only one part of comfort.
picture: Presenter holds shoe at chest height; camera moves closer.
notes: Small music dip emphasizes the change in argument. This is the first explanatory reset.

vo: How does that particular pair feel when you turn?
picture: Low three-quarter shot: wearer makes an ordinary controlled turn in a hallway.
notes: Follow the feet in real time; no staged wobble or unsafe instability.

vo: When you take the stairs?
picture: Side shot of two normal steps with a handrail available.
notes: Match shoe model and clothing to previous row. Do not ask talent to provoke pain.

vo: When you walk around your kitchen instead of straight down a store aisle?
picture: Wide home kitchen shot: woman walks from counter to cupboard. Brief match cut from a straight showroom walk if available.
notes: End on the home setting. Different task, not a before/after medical result.

vo: If the shoe feels awkward or unsteady on your feet, don’t ignore that because someone else loves it.
picture: Presenter, then close-up of wearer thoughtfully checking fit while seated. A small 'How does it feel to YOU?' card can replace a second footage cut.
notes: Keep 'if' in captions. No claim that Hoka universally creates instability; no fabricated fall.

vo: You’re the one who has to wear it through the day.
picture: Woman places keys beside shoes at the door; hold a natural, quiet moment.
notes: Finish Hoka section with personal relevance, not a danger animation.

vo: Number two, New Balance walking shoes.
picture: Same number-card layout, now real New Balance walking model.
notes: Match visual treatment and sound cue to number one. Identify the actual model internally; do not mix different models in the sequence.

vo: A familiar name. A sensible-looking choice.
picture: Clean side profile, then an ordinary mirror try-on.
notes: Short acknowledgement before the fit objection, matching the reference’s concession-first rhythm.

vo: But the name on the side doesn’t tell you whether you’ve chosen the right fit.
picture: Close-up of shoe logo; rack focus or cut to the front of the shoe.
notes: Guide the eye from branding to fit; do not cross out or deform the logo.

vo: Look at what’s happening around your toes.
picture: Top-down view of wearer’s forefoot inside the shoe. Hand indicates the front gently.
notes: Use a simple outline around the actual toe box. Do not fabricate an X-ray through a competitor shoe.

vo: Do they have room? Or are they pressing against each other?
picture: Neutral diagram of a foot outline within two generic fit outlines: adequate space versus crowded space. Clearly label 'Fit illustration'; keep competitor logos off this diagram.
notes: Show a fit principle, not a claim that every New Balance is narrow. No painful toe deformation.

vo: Does the upper feel comfortable across your foot? Or are you loosening the laces by lunchtime?
picture: Close-up of seated wearer adjusting laces normally; cut to a kitchen clock for the lunchtime cue.
notes: Keep wearer seated. One action across two camera angles; no swelling transformation.

vo: New Balance makes different models and widths. The pair that works for your friend may fit you completely differently.
picture: Presenter at table; cut to two distinct, accurately labeled model/width boxes only if available, otherwise use simple text 'MODEL + WIDTH + FIT'.
notes: Do not fake width labels, inventory, reviews, or a recommendation from a friend.

vo: When you’re already dealing with back and leg pain, the last thing you want is a shoe adding pressure and rubbing to your feet.
picture: Woman checks a shoe seam with fingers while seated; macro of fabric contact. Generic shoe for any pressure illustration, with no invented sores or skin damage.
notes: Keep this about local foot comfort. Do not animate a pressure wave traveling to the spine.

vo: Number three, Brooks Ghost or Adrenaline.
picture: Number card with Ghost and Adrenaline packshots, each accurately labeled. If only one is sourced, show that model while both are named in voiceover.
notes: Same card system; no 'VS' unless actually comparing the two models.

vo: These are often on the shortlist when someone decides to invest in a better pair of shoes.
picture: Woman compares shoe boxes or looks at the pair on a shop bench; cut to clean product detail.
notes: No fabricated price tag, sales data, or review score.

vo: But don’t let a comfortable walk around the shop make the whole decision.
picture: Show a short, ordinary showroom walk, then presenter.
notes: Cut on 'whole decision'. Maintain neutral treatment of the shoe.

vo: What about standing at the kitchen counter?
picture: Medium side shot of woman preparing tea at the counter; feet visible.
notes: Hold 2–3 seconds; no pain acting needed.

vo: Waiting in the grocery line?
picture: Wide or medium licensed supermarket queue scene with adult woman and basket.
notes: Keep stock footage natural. Avoid private bystanders in newly filmed footage unless cleared.

vo: Walking for a while, sitting down, and getting up again?
picture: Three matched shots: hallway walk, sitting in a chair, ordinary rise from the same chair. Keep the same outfit and footwear.
notes: Three actions, three cuts. Do not present the rise as a treatment result.

vo: Those are the moments your shoes need to fit into.
picture: Presenter looks to camera, with a quick return to the everyday activity.
notes: Brief explanatory reset after the activity montage.

vo: If a pair feels good for ten minutes but leaves your feet uncomfortable later, the brand name doesn’t change that experience.
picture: Seated woman considers shoes at end of day; cut to a simple 10 MINUTES → LATER card. No before/after body graphics.
notes: Keep conditional wording visible. Do not turn this into a universal claim about Brooks.

vo: So where does ComfortWear fit in?
picture: Full-screen clinic presenter; clear other shoes from the framing and reach toward ComfortWear.
notes: Allow a brief pause. This is the main transition; use a subtle music lift.

vo: They’re called ComfortWear Ortho Stretch Cushion Shoes.
picture: Hero product shot on a neutral table: actual black/purple or navy/blue Ortho Stretch pair. Cut to in-hand three-quarter view.
notes: Hold product name long enough to read. Use the exact real shoe, not an HF-like generated substitute.

vo: They aren’t a treatment for sciatica. They’re an option for everyday foot comfort while you follow your clinician’s treatment plan.
picture: Presenter calmly delivers the line with ComfortWear beside them. No pain-resolution imagery. Caption the complete line at ordinary size and speed.
notes: Do not rush, hide, or contradict this line with anatomy animation or testimonials.
ref: Replaces the reference’s treatment claim at 1:58–2:00

vo: Here’s what they offer.
picture: Presenter rotates the shoe to start a practical demonstration.
notes: Cut on hand movement into the first feature.

vo: A wide toe box gives your toes room instead of crowding them together.
picture: Top-down actual ComfortWear shoe. Trace its forefoot outline with a thin blue stroke; cut to fingers indicating its width. Optional neutral foot-outline fit diagram sized to the actual shoe.
notes: No numeric width claim, oversized toe spread, or competitor compression comparison.

vo: A stretchy knit upper provides a more forgiving fit across the top of your foot.
picture: Macro: two fingers gently pull and release the knit across the forefoot. Repeat once in real time; match to wearer’s shoe.
notes: Use real material behavior. Do not claim swelling disappears or circulation improves.

vo: A supportive insole sits underneath your arches, with cushioning under the heel to soften each step.
picture: First show actual insole contour, only removing it if the real product allows removal. Then close-up of heel cushion under normal finger pressure; finish with a normal heel-to-toe walking shot.
notes: Two feature labels appear sequentially. If using a diagram, keep it confined to foot/shoe and match the product; no invented layer count or spine realignment.

vo: And the lightweight design means less bulk on your feet as you move through your day.
picture: Hand lifts one shoe easily, then low tracking shot of normal walking.
notes: No fake scale reading, weight comparison, or floating shoe stunt.

vo: The material is breathable, too, with a slip-resistant outsole for everyday grip.
picture: Macro knit texture with small airflow icons labeled 'Illustration'; flip the actual shoe to show tread, then walk on a dry ordinary floor.
notes: Do not film a wet-floor stunt, claim slip-proof performance, or use an invented traction test.

vo: Room around your toes. Support under your feet. A comfortable fit you don’t have to spend the afternoon thinking about.
picture: Three-beat recap: top-down toe box, actual insole, woman wearing shoes while reading at a café or chatting.
notes: Cut each of the first two nouns to its matching feature; hold the final lifestyle beat.

vo: Because when you’re already managing sciatica, you don’t need uncomfortable shoes demanding your attention as well.
picture: Presenter returns for the emotional bridge; then wearer steps away from the shoe rack.
notes: Maintain the distinction between foot comfort and the condition being managed.

vo: You want to get dressed, get out the door, and focus on the things you planned to do.
picture: Woman puts on coat, picks up keys, and exits the front door in ComfortWear.
notes: Three connected actions. Show ordinary shoe entry if included; no unsupported hands-free feature.

vo: The grocery run. Lunch with your sister. An afternoon with the grandchildren.
picture: Three lifestyle clips: carrying a light grocery bag; seated outdoor lunch with another adult woman; walking at an easy pace beside a grandchild.
notes: Aspirational lifestyle montage, not a testimonial or proof of sciatica recovery. Obtain appropriate releases for any children filmed.

vo: Before you buy another pair based only on the logo or how soft it feels in the store, take a closer look at the fit and features.
picture: Presenter beside the shoe; cut through toe-box, upper and insole details once more.
notes: Keep the final criteria consistent with opening; no new feature claims here.

vo: You can explore ComfortWear Ortho Stretch Cushion Shoes at the link below.
picture: Pair on clean table, brand name and product title. Lower-screen CTA; end on actual shoes with a subtle camera push.
overlay: EXPLORE ORTHO STRETCH / TAP TO SHOP
notes: Keep final card 3–4 seconds, extending picture after voiceover if needed. No unverified discount, trial period or clinic seal.
